item.title: Finding Integer Roots of Polynomials in Nearly Optimal Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.04730v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Let $f\in\mathbb Z[x]$ be a polynomial of degree $n$ with integer coefficients of absolute value less than $2^b$. Using Pan's approximate factorization theorem, we give a deterministic algorithm that finds all distinct integer roots of $f$ in $\widetilde O(nb)$ bit operations. This matches the bit size of the input up to logarithmic factors and does not require $f$ to be square-free. Since we were unable to verify parts of the running time analysis of Pan's theorem, we also give a self-contained deterministic algorithm with running time $\widetilde O(nb+\min(n,b)^3b^2)$, which is $\widetilde O(nb)$ whenever $b\leq n^{1/4}$. This answers a question of Harvey and Hittmeir (2022), who asked whether integer roots can be found deterministically in quasilinear time, conditionally on Pan's theorem, and unconditionally for $b\leq n^{1/4}$. The fastest previous deterministic algorithm, due to Nir, takes $\widetilde O(n^{3/2}b)$ bit operations and works only for square-free polynomials. Instead of $p$-adic lifting, we combine approximate complex root finding with exact polynomial evaluation. We first approximate the complex roots of the polynomial formed by the top $\min(n,b)+1$ coefficients of $f$. Every integer root $r$ of $f$ with $|r|\geq 2$ lies within distance $2$ of some complex root of this truncated polynomial. Rounding the real parts of the approximate roots therefore gives a list of $O(\min(n,b))$ candidate integers that is guaranteed to contain all integer roots of $f$. Although a single candidate can have up to $b$ bits, a bound via the Mahler measure shows that the bit lengths of all candidates sum to $O(b)$. This allows us to test all candidates by exact multipoint evaluation in $\widetilde O(nb)$ bit operations.
item.dc:creator: Yansong Feng, Itamar Nir

item.title: ALBI: LLM-Guided Inductive Logic Programming via Iterative Generate-Test-Constrain Refineme
item.description: arXiv:2611.05039v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce ALBI (Agent for Learning By Induction), a neuro-symbolic ILP framework that replaces the ASP-based hypothesis generator in the Learning from Failures (LFF) paradigm with a Large Language Model (LLM), while retaining SWI-Prolog as a formal verifier. ALBI implements an iterative generate-test-constrain loop: the LLM proposes candidate hypotheses from structured prompts; Prolog tests each candidate; and diagnostic feedback drives refinement. We further introduce semantic anonymization, a metamorphic testing methodology, to distinguish structural symbolic induction from surface-level pattern matching on predicate names. Experiments on 30 standard ILP benchmarks show that ALBI achieves 100% success across three frontier LLMs (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT 5.4 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6), matching Popper while requiring only 1.4-1.7 iterations on average. Under anonymization, all models maintain 100% success with a moderate iteration increase (1.36-1.67 times), providing evidence of robust symbolic reasoning.
item.dc:creator: Aboubaker Seddiq Benterki, J\"uri Vain, Gert Kanter, Leelo Aino J\"urgenstein

item.title: Some algebraic and geometric computations in CH via Chow forms
item.description: arXiv:2611.05289v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The problem of decomposing an algebraic variety into more structured components (such as equidimensional, irreducible, or connected components) is a fundamental problem in computer algebra and algebraic geometry. In this work, we study the computational complexity of computing equidimensional components of algebraic varieties, represented via Chow forms. We improve the state-of-the-art complexity bounds from PSPACE to CH, the counting hierarchy, for a number of problems related to equidimensional decomposition, including deciding (1) whether the Chow form of the $k^{\text{th}}$ equidimensional component of a given projective variety vanishes at a given point, (2) whether a given monomial is in the support of the Chow form of the $k^{\text{th}}$ equidimensional component of a given projective variety, (3) membership in a given equidimensional component of a given algebraic variety, and (4) membership in the closure of the image of an irreducible variety under a polynomial map. As an application of our algorithm to decide membership in the closure of the image of a variety under a polynomial map, we show that the approximate polynomial satisfiability problem can be decided in CH. We also show that the degree of the $k^{\text{th}}$ equidimensional component of a given projective variety can be computed in $\text{FP}^{\text{CH}}$. Our main technical result is the construction of a polylogtime-uniform family of constant-depth, exponential-size threshold circuits that compute the Chow forms of the equidimensional components of a given projective variety. We construct these circuits by combining the machinery of geometric resolutions together with the uniform constant-depth, exponential-size threshold circuits of Andrews, Garg, and Schost (FOCS 2026) for the multivariate resultant.
item.dc:creator: Robert Andrews, Abhibhav Garg, Rafael Oliveira, \'Eric Schost

item.title: A Quantitative Approach to Reach-Avoid Reachability Analysis for Discrete-Time Nonlinear Control Systems
item.description: arXiv:2511.15238v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A reach-avoid specification requires a dynamical system to reach a target set of states while avoiding a failure set. Reachability analysis partitions the state space into parts starting from which the specification can be satisfied by following some control signal and those from which it cannot despite the best control effort. In this paper, we present a quantitative approach for reachability analysis to analyze the satisfaction of avoid and reach-avoid specifications for discrete-time nonlinear control systems. In such an approach, a value function assigns a value to each state that determines how robustly the system can satisfy the specification starting from it and following the optimal control signal. However, computing such a value function is difficult. Instead, our approach constructs discrete abstractions on which it performs value iteration to compute sound bounds on the desired value function. The resulting lower bound enables a sound under-approximation of the reach avoid set (RAS) and, in the avoid case, a sound over-approximation of the backward reachable set (BRS). When the control set is finite, the upper bound additionally enables a sound over-approximation of the RAS and, in the avoid case, a sound under-approximation of the BRS. The lower bound also yields quantitative guarantees on safety margins and safe target-reaching times. Our approach further refines the abstraction by splitting the grid cells that could not be classified as within or outside the BRS (or RAS) to improve the usefulness of the bounds. We evaluate our approach on five example systems with up to five-dimensional state spaces.
item.dc:creator: Ihab Tabbara, Eliya Badr, Hussein Sibai

item.title: Quantifier Elimination Meets Treewidth
item.description: arXiv:2601.00312v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we address the complexity barrier inherent in Fourier-Motzkin elimination (FME) and cylindrical algebraic decomposition (CAD) when eliminating a block of (existential) quantifiers. To mitigate this, we propose exploiting structural sparsity in the variable dependency graph of quantified formulas. Utilizing tools from parameterized algorithms, we investigate the role of treewidth, a parameter that measures the graph's tree-likeness, in the process of quantifier elimination. A novel dynamic programming framework, structured over a tree decomposition of the dependency graph, is developed for applying FME and CAD, and is also extensible to general quantifier elimination procedures. Crucially, we prove that when the treewidth is a constant, the framework achieves a significant exponential complexity improvement for both FME and CAD, reducing the worst-case complexity bound from doubly exponential to single exponential. Preliminary experiments on sparse linear real arithmetic (LRA) and nonlinear real arithmetic (NRA) benchmarks confirm that our algorithm outperforms the existing popular heuristic-based approaches on instances exhibiting low treewidth.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wu, Jiyu Zhu, Amir Kafshdar Goharshady, Jie An, Bican Xia, Naijun Zhan
